source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (Psychological Review 117:994-1024)
finding: Explicit-Implicit Interaction (EII) theory has five principles: explicit and implicit knowledge co-exist and differ; most tasks use both at once; the two are redundantly represented; their outputs are integrated; processing is iterative and can run both ways. Wallas stages map on: preparation and verification are mostly explicit, incubation is mostly implicit, insight is an explicitation step.
numbers: Five core principles plus auxiliary ones (e.g. confidence thresholds on an Internal Confidence Level, ICL). Simulated with the CLARION architecture on 4 phenomena: lexical decision priming, free-recall reminiscence, Durso knowledge graphs, coin-problem overshadowing.
limits: Insight is treated as ordinary two-level processing whose implicit part is hidden from awareness, not as a special mechanism. The model is fitted to published human data, not tested on new data.
agent_relevance: Supports a scaffold with two channels: a cheap associative generator (implicit) and a rule checker (explicit), integrated by a confidence threshold. Matches the schema split of generation versus checking.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (Psychological Review 117:994-1024) - Darwinian mapping
finding: EII casts creative search as three Darwin-like steps: blind-ish variation (implicit hypothesis generation by noisy association), selection (evaluation against the ICL), retention (the selected association is output or used as new input). The authors say the model captures the blind-variation process, but through soft-constraint satisfaction, not pure chance.
numbers: Bottom level: neural network settling (Hopfield-style soft constraints); top level: explicit rules that only give stereotyped responses. Boltzmann noise parameter changes between phases (a lower value to refocus search).
limits: Differs from Gabora's honing theory, which rejects the variation-selection frame. The two theories disagree on this exact point.
agent_relevance: Variation then selection is a recipe for S3 generate / S4 test. Noise (temperature) is the knob: raise it at an impasse, lower it to refocus.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (Psychological Review 117:994-1024) - rare-word association and lexical decision (Yaniv & Meyer 1987 data)
finding: People who failed to recall a rare word but felt close (high feeling of knowing, FOK) still recognised the target faster later. CLARION reproduced it: priming after correct answers, none after incorrect ones, FOK-dependent effect when no answer was given.
numbers: Humans: 44 participants, 52 rare-word association trials, 312 lexical decision trials; correct trial priming t(2100)=8.5, p<.001; incorrect trial t(2100)=0.7 n.s. Simulation: correct t(2976)=6.87 p<.0001; incorrect t(2221)=1.91 n.s.; FOK ANOVA F(2,5998)=42.87.
limits: Human numbers are from the 1987 study as re-analysed by the authors. Simulated N is thousands, so p-values are not comparable to human power.
agent_relevance: Partial activation below the answer threshold is useful: the agent can keep near-miss candidates and re-use them rather than discard them (an FOK-like score).

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (Psychological Review 117:994-1024) - free-recall reminiscence (Smith & Vela 1991 data)
finding: Recall of new items on a second test rises with the length of the break after the first test (an incubation-like effect). CLARION reproduced the pattern; test length had no effect in either.
numbers: Humans: incubation interval F(3,209)=9.4, p<.01; mean reminiscence 2.90, 3.15, 3.72, 5.00 for 0, 1, 5, 10 min; test duration F(2,209)=.27 n.s. Model: interval F(3,11998)=1661.34, p<.0001; test duration F(2,11988)=0.78 n.s.
limits: Effect confined to the first minute of the second test (Smith & Vela, as cited). It is memory consolidation, not problem solving.
agent_relevance: Break time helps recall of already-seen items. An LLM has no clock; resampling after a context change is the nearest analogue.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (Psychological Review 117:994-1024) - overshadowing in the coin problem (Schooler et al. 1993)
finding: Asking solvers to verbalise their strategy mid-way hurt insight solutions compared with an unrelated task. CLARION matched this: verbalisation shuts down implicit hypothesis generation.
numbers: Humans (82 participants, 2 min then 90 s interruption): 45.8% solved after an unrelated task vs 35.6% after verbalising, t(74)=2.13, p<.05, about 30% relative drop. Model, 5000 runs each: 45.3% vs 35.3%, binomial p<.0001; fit error under 0.5 points.
limits: One problem (the coin). Verbal overshadowing of insight has not been found in every study (see the Chein & Weisberg line).
agent_relevance: Forcing written reasoning during an impasse could cost associative search. Test a silent resample step at the impasse versus an explain-your-reasoning step.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (Psychological Review 117:994-1024) - Durso et al. 1994 knowledge graphs (hiccup riddle)
finding: Solvers of the bartender-and-shotgun riddle had a restructured knowledge graph: the focal point moved from Bartender to Relieved. The model reproduced it as a shift in implicit associations.
numbers: 12 participants, 2 hours of yes/no questions, half solved; solver and non-solver graphs differed by 12 edges; correlation between graphs about zero. Original gave no further statistics.
limits: Tiny sample, no inferential statistics in the source.
agent_relevance: Restructuring is a changed association graph, not a changed search order. Representation change belongs in S2.

source: Helie, Sun & Xiong (2008) Mixed effects of distractor tasks on incubation (CogSci proceedings)
finding: The literature on distractor tasks during incubation was inconsistent. CLARION predicted that a distractor hurts in proportion to how much it uses explicit resources. A human free-recall experiment confirmed it: explicit-heavy distractors cut reminiscence below the no-incubation level.
numbers: 114 undergraduates, 6 groups of 19. Reminiscence: Do Nothing 7.26 > No Incubation 4.9 = Remote Association 4.84 = Perceptual-Motor 4.84 > Syllogistic 2.47 = Dynamic Control 2.26; F(5,108)=10.65, p<.001.
limits: One main task (free recall). Prediction for insight tasks not tested here.
agent_relevance: Rest helps, load hurts. Any think-about-something-else step must be low in demand or it harms the incubation it is meant to give.

source: Dodds, Ward & Smith (2003) review of incubation experiments, as cited in Helie, Sun & Xiong (2008)
finding: Review of 39 incubation experiments: 29 found a significant effect. Longer incubation and preparatory activity help; useful clues in the break help, misleading clues harm. Effects of distractor type, expertise and gender are unstable. Olton & Johnson (1976) used seven distractor types on insight problems and found no incubation effect.
numbers: 29 of 39 experiments positive (as cited).
limits: Second-hand: I read only the citing paper.
agent_relevance: Incubation is real in about three quarters of studies but fragile; do not rely on it as the only source of variation.

source: Helie & Sun (2009) Simulating incubation effects using the EII-BF (Bayes factor) model (IJCNN)
finding: A neural-network version of EII in which implicit and explicit steps alternate, and a Bayes factor decides when an implicit association is confident enough to output. It simulates incubation in lexical decision and free recall.
numbers: Bayes factor reading used: under 3.2 not worth mentioning, over 10 strong, over 100 decisive.
limits: Skimmed intro and method only. Same two tasks as the Psychological Review paper.
agent_relevance: A Bayes-factor style confidence gate on a candidate is a concrete, code-checkable selector (fits G5).

source: RPI press release (2010) New psychology theory enables computers to mimic human creativity (ScienceDaily)
finding: Popular summary of the Helie & Sun coin-problem result; numbers match the paper.
limits: Press, no new data.
agent_relevance: None beyond the coin-problem line.

source: Gabora (2017) Honing theory: a complex systems framework for creativity (Nonlinear Dynamics, Psychology & Life Sciences 21:35-88)
finding: Honing theory: creativity starts when the mind meets high psychological-entropy material and recursively re-views it from new contexts until it is restructured and arousal drops. Creative thought is not search and select over discrete candidates; the idea is one half-baked potentiality state that is honed. It is explicitly non-Darwinian and set against BVSR.
numbers: Claims: restructuring needs neural synchrony and a shift to associative mode; the formalism borrows quantum-style superposition and context-driven state change for concept combination.
quote: creativity involves not searching and selecting amongst well-formed idea candidates but amalgamating and honing information from multiple sources
limits: Mostly a framework. The quantum-style formalism is a metaphor for brain processes (the paper says it is unrelated to quantum-brain claims). Empirical support is from the same lab with small samples.
agent_relevance: Counter-idea to generate-many-then-pick: keep one fuzzy draft and re-view it in new contexts. Test N parallel attempts versus one attempt re-contextualised N times at equal tokens.

source: Gabora & Saab (2011) Creative interference and states of potentiality in analogy problem solving (CogSci), as reported in Gabora (2017)
finding: Participants working Gick & Holyoak's General/Radiation problem were interrupted midway and asked what they were thinking. Responses showing merged sources with unweeded extra information (honing) were commoner than responses showing one clean selected source being mapped (structure mapping).
numbers: Honing judgments had significantly higher frequency count and mean than structure-mapping judgments (N and statistics not given in the review I read).
limits: Second-hand inside the 2017 review; the original is not opened. Coded by judges; no numbers in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Mid-process LLM drafts may also be blends of several sources; check whether the model really picks one source and maps it.

source: Carbert, Gabora, Schwartz & Ranjan (2014) Cognitive states of potentiality in art-making (AIEA Congress)
finding: Undergraduates painted something that expressed themselves, were interrupted midway and asked whether all their ideas were distinct and separate. Judges classed answers as honing-type (single ill-defined idea) or search-and-select-type. More answers were classed as honing.
numbers: 56 artists, 11 judges; an answer counted as H or S if 6+ judges agreed. 29 H vs 13 S, one-sample chi-square(1, N=43)=4.57, p<.05. ICC for the Form D question .94; two other questions had ICC too low and were dropped. Mean-judgment test t(55)=2.64, p<.05, effect .38; the printed means (S 9.67, H 4.35) look inconsistent with an H win, probably a labelling slip.
limits: Weak test: one self-report question, judges taught both theories first, p just under .05, no replication by another lab found.
agent_relevance: Evidence that humans hold a single unfinished idea is thin. Do not build on it alone.

source: Gabora (2019) Reframing convergent and divergent thought for the 21st century (CogSci proceedings)
finding: Argues the usual definitions (convergent = one right answer, divergent = many answers) are inconsistent. Proposes convergent thought = concepts viewed from conventional contexts, divergent = viewed from unconventional contexts, both points on one honing process.
numbers: No new data. Uses AUT fluency, originality, flexibility and the RAT as examples.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: The agent can vary the context frame instead of the sample count: same problem, conventional frame then unconventional frame.

source: Gabora (2017) - EVOC computational model of cultural evolution (as summarised in the honing theory paper)
finding: Neural-network agents invent or imitate actions. Culture improves best with a mix of inventing and imitating, about 2 invent : 1 imitate; too much invention wastes effort on reinventing.
numbers: Best mean fitness at a creating-to-imitating ratio of about 2:1; with a creators/imitators split there is a trade-off between share of creators and how creative they are; agents that self-regulated creativity did better than ones that did not (Gabora & Tseng 2014).
limits: Toy simulation; the author notes it may say little about real societies.
agent_relevance: In multi-sample search, balance new ideas against copying the best so far. A fixed explore:exploit ratio near 2:1 is a candidate default to test (a design guess).

source: Gabora (2017) - style recognition across domains (Gabora, O'Connor & Ranjan 2012; Ranjan 2014), as reported in the honing theory paper
finding: Art students and writing students could pick which unseen works were made by a given creator, even across domains, at above chance.
numbers: Reported only as significantly above chance; no counts given.
limits: Second-hand, no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Supports same model, same fingerprint: samples from one model share style, so they are not independent (G4).

source: Gabora (2017) - cross-domain translation of ideas and authenticity (Ranjan et al. 2013; Henderson & Gabora 2013), as reported
finding: Participants matched paintings to the music that inspired them above chance; raters agreed on the authenticity of dance and stand-up performances (positive correlation).
numbers: 3 expert painters, 4 paintings from 4 music pieces; matching significantly above chance (statistic not shown). Authenticity ratings across viewers significantly positively correlated.
limits: Tiny stimulus sets; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Weak relevance.

source: Weisberg (2015) Toward an integrated theory of insight in problem solving (Thinking & Reasoning 21:5-39), as characterised by later papers
finding: Weisberg business-as-usual view: insight arises mainly from conscious, effortful analytic operations, with restructuring as a distinguishing feature; unconscious processes enter only at an impasse. Impasse is not required for insight.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Known only through descriptions in Stuyck et al. 2022, Chein & Weisberg 2014 and a search summary. Original not read.
agent_relevance: Supports insight is ordinary: the agent may not need a special insight mode, just more varied ordinary steps.

source: Chein & Weisberg (2014) Working memory and insight in verbal problems: analysis of compound remote associates (Memory & Cognition 42:67-83)
finding: Weisberg-side test of the business-as-usual theory. Solutions rated as insight were common, and insight solutions correlated with verbal working memory and attention control. Insight solutions were faster than analytic ones, opposite to a special-process prediction. No verbal overshadowing from thinking aloud.
numbers: N=53 (think-aloud 27, silent 26); solved 42% of 60 CRA items; 64% of solved items rated partly or fully insight (35% full, 28% partial), 36% analytic. Verbal WM predicted overall CRA beta=.40, t=2.25, p=.03; spatial WM bivariate r(52)=.28 vanished when verbal WM was controlled (beta=.04). Insight vs analytic solution time t(51)=8.0, p<.001.
limits: Correlational, student sample, CRA word items only. WM did not correlate with items rated analytic, an unexpected null that the authors flag.
agent_relevance: Even insightful solutions use the same limited-capacity control. Do not starve the agent of working context during an impasse.

source: Stuyck, Cleeremans & Van den Bussche (2022) Aha! under pressure: the Aha! experience is not constrained by cognitive load (Cognition)
finding: Dual-task test of Weisberg's claim that insight uses limited conscious resources. Load cut non-insight solutions but left insight solutions unaffected, against the strict business-as-usual view.
numbers: N=106, 70 word puzzles. Insight solutions were more accurate (94% vs 77%, d=-1.57) and more confident (.79 vs .66). Correct counts: insight 18.0 vs non-insight 11.4. For non-insight, correct count no-load 15.8 vs high-load 7.9 (d=0.66); for insight, no difference between load levels (all p>.69).
limits: Self-reported insight, word puzzles only, high-load data heavily trimmed (25% extra exclusions). Authors note the result also fits an integrated view.
agent_relevance: Associative (insight-type) solutions are robust under load; analytic ones are not. For an LLM, short fast associative samples are probably cheap and robust, long chain reasoning is the load-sensitive part.

source: Insight problem solving is not that special, but business is not quite as usual (PMC10366031, 2023)
finding: Tested special-process vs business-as-usual with four problem types under silence, articulatory suppression and spatial tapping. Insight problems resembled spatial non-insight problems, were not hurt by secondary tasks, and drew on analogical and convergent thinking more than divergent thinking. Authors endorse an unequal mix: mostly ordinary, with a rare exceptional route.
numbers: Exact N not extracted this session.
limits: Abstract and introduction read only.
agent_relevance: Convergent and analogical skill predicts insight, divergent fluency little. Argues for selecting on convergent checks, not volume of ideas.

source: Kershaw & Ohlsson (2001) Training for insight: the case of the nine-dot problem (CogSci)
finding: Nine-dot difficulty comes from prior-knowledge constraints (do not turn on non-dot points, do not cross lines, stay in the figure). Training that relaxes them lifts solving; training that adds them hinders. Cites Burnham & Davis 1969 and Weisberg & Alba 1981: telling people to go outside the square only helps when combined with a hint giving part of the solution.
numbers: Baseline nine-dot solving under 5% in a few minutes (Lung & Dominowski 1985; MacGregor et al. 2001). N=90: facilitating group 19/30 (63%) solved the first insight problem, hindering 8/30 (27%), no training 11/30 (37%), chi-square(2,N=90)=8.836, p<.05. Among those who completed training, 17/19 (89%) solved vs 2/11 (18%) of those who did not, chi-square(1,N=30)=15.248.
limits: The training-completion split is post hoc. Weisberg & Alba's own numbers are only known second-hand.
agent_relevance: Difficulty is wrongly applied ordinary knowledge. Fix it by naming and relaxing the assumed constraint, which is what a drop-one-assumption operator does.

source: Weisberg & Alba (1981) An examination of the alleged role of fixation in the solution of several insight problems (JEP: General), as cited
finding: Nine-dot: the hint to draw outside the square alone did not reliably produce solutions; hints giving the first line did better. A web summary says solution rose to 62% with first line plus outside hint, and was 20-25% across two experiments with only the outside hint.
numbers: The 20-25% and 62% figures come from a web summary and a book review; unverified.
limits: Not read. Treat all figures as unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: Insight failure is not fixation that one nudge lifts; it needs a structural hint.

source: Beucler & De Neys (2026, accepted in Cognition) Intuitive insight: fast associative processes drive sound creative thinking
finding: Two-response paradigm on compound remote associates under load and deadline. Most correct final answers were already correct as fast first answers. LLM embeddings and semantic-network models predicted which items were solved intuitively: items with a smaller semantic search space, and people with more connected, less fragmented semantic networks.
numbers: Two experiments, 100 participants each, 24 CRA items. Initial accuracy 48.3% and 49.8%; final 65.2% and 66.7%; d=0.35. Non-correction rate 72.7% and 71.4% (share of final correct answers already correct at first response). Trials excluded for missing the deadline or load check: 20.1% and 36.7%. Cue-to-solution embedding similarity correlated with intuitive correct rate r(22)=.54 in both. Network measures from a separate fluency sample: Hedges g=0.61 for clustering, -0.66 for modularity.
limits: Convergent word problems only. Tight deadlines still leave imperfect control of deliberation; the high exclusion rate may favour easy trials.
agent_relevance: Strong support: most good answers need no long deliberation. Fits G11 (short attempts) and a fast associative first guess with a code-checked verifier; deliberation fixes only about 28% of correct finals.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI delivers creative output but struggles with thinking processes (arXiv 2503.23327)
finding: Compared GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4 and GPT-4o with Chinese undergraduates over 8 experiments. LLMs beat humans on divergent thinking, remote associates and some insight tasks, lost on creative writing, free-association distance and representational-change items. Authors argue the insight accuracy likely comes from probabilistic inference over prior knowledge, not restructuring.
numbers: Insight tasks (about 60 humans): Chinese character puzzle, humans beat GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 but lost to GPT-4o (-0.21 accuracy estimate); stumpers, GPT-4o above humans by 0.06 (p=.011); rebus, GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o above humans by 0.32 and 0.39. Representational change task: humans higher than GPT-4-turbo by 0.46 and GPT-4o by 0.31 (both p<.001); LLMs chose by reasoning 68.9% (GPT-4o) and 71.3% (GPT-4-turbo), humans by transformation 72.4%. Free association: humans farther from the prompt and higher forward flow than all three models.
limits: Older models; one language and culture; representational-change task is forced choice, not free generation; puzzle contamination not checked.
agent_relevance: LLMs may solve stored insight puzzles by recall; real restructuring looks weaker. Do not assume the model restructures; give it an explicit operator and test on held-out puzzle forms (G3).

source: Orru et al. (2023) and Raz et al. (2024), cited in Zhang et al. 2025 for LLM insight performance
finding: Orru et al. report GPT-3 comparable to humans on verbal insight tasks; Raz et al. report GPT-4 significantly better than humans on similar tasks.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand through Zhang et al.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo, arXiv 2509.14704)
finding: Insight-riddle benchmark. Frontier models far below humans, and reasoning in Japanese did not help. Many models produced the right answer in their thought log and then failed to endorse it (verification failure).
numbers: 201 riddles; 120-item human comparison subset. Non-reasoning models (n=16) 7.60%, reasoning models (n=19) 17.59%, humans 52.9%. Per-model rates in the full set include Grok-4 37.6%, Claude Opus 4 30.3%, DeepSeek R1-0528 22.9%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 10.9%. GPT-5 is the stated exception near human level.
limits: Japanese wordplay; search-augmented models scored near human, so contamination is possible for them; thought logs read by hand.
agent_relevance: Models fail at recognising a correct idea, not only at producing it. Select by an external check (G5, G8), do not trust the model's own sense of being right.

source: Han et al. (2025, NeurIPS) Creativity or brute force? Brainteasers as a window into LLM problem solving (arXiv 2505.10844)
finding: Braingle brainteaser benchmark graded for correctness and for whether the solution used a short creative insight or brute-force search. LLMs often find the insight, but all models sometimes fall back on brute force when a shorter path exists. Math framing and hints lower brute-force use.
numbers: 478 problems (242 math, 236 logic). o3 scored 88.8% on the Math set with hints plus math prompt, 80.5% on the hardest 50. o3 judgments agreed with human labels 99.3% (correctness) and 97% (creative vs brute). Brute-force use falls with model size.
limits: The judge is itself an LLM (checked against humans at 97-99%); brute force defined as code, exhaustive search or guess-and-check; some problems may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Fits the ordinary-process story: models take the cheap ordinary route unless pushed. A hint or a restate-as-math step lowers brute force, so an impasse operator that reframes the problem is worth testing.

source: Simonton BVSR versus ordinary-cognition critiques, as presented in Gabora (2017) and Helie & Sun (2010)
finding: Campbell/Simonton blind variation and selective retention (BVSR) was radically reformulated by Simonton (2012) to allow sightedness (guided variation); Gabora argues this is no longer clearly Darwinian. Helie & Sun treat BVSR as compatible with EII (soft, guided variation). So Weisberg, Helie & Sun, and Gabora disagree on whether search-and-select is the right frame.
numbers: No numbers; theory conflict.
limits: Positions are summarised by the rival theorists. No neutral review opened.
agent_relevance: Open design question: variation-and-selection loop (EII, BVSR) versus single-draft re-contextualisation (honing). Run both at equal tokens (G7).
